questions.question: Q: What do the Lotus-Eaters symbolise in the Odyssey?

points.text: They represent the temptation of forgetting — abandoning the struggle of life and the journey home for passive comfort and oblivion. Those who eat the lotus lose all desire to return.

questions.question: Q: Why must Odysseus choose between Scylla and Charybdis?

points.text: They are positioned on opposite sides of a narrow strait. Avoiding Charybdis (the whirlpool that destroys the whole ship) means sailing close to Scylla (who takes six men). There is no safe path — only a least-worst choice.

questions.question: Q: How does Circe differ from Calypso as a threat?

points.text: Circe is an active danger who transforms men into animals; Calypso is a passive temptation who offers comfort and immortality. Circe threatens the body; Calypso threatens the will to continue.

questions.question: Q: Why does Odysseus want to hear the Sirens?

points.text: Curiosity and desire for knowledge — the Sirens promise knowledge of all things. His solution (being tied to the mast) shows he wants to experience the temptation without succumbing to it.

questions.question: Q: What does the loss of Odysseus's entire crew suggest about his leadership?

points.text: Despite his cleverness, Odysseus cannot save everyone. His crew's disobedience (opening the bag of winds, killing the Cattle of the Sun) and his own errors (revealing his name to Polyphemus) all contribute to their deaths.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: The monsters of the Odyssey represent challenges to Odysseus's identity far more than mere physical threats, though the physical danger is real and deadly. The Lotus-Eaters threaten Odysseus's identity as a man driven by purpose — their fruit erases the desire for homecoming, making the journey meaningless. The Cyclops challenges Odysseus's identity as a civilised Greek — Polyphemus ignores xenia, eats men raw and mocks the gods, representing everything Odysseus is not. Defeating him requires metis (cunning), Odysseus's defining quality, but revealing his name afterwards shows a failure of the self-control that is equally part of his heroic identity. The Sirens challenge Odysseus as a seeker of knowledge — he wants to hear them but must ensure he does not lose himself to their song. Circe and Calypso challenge Odysseus's identity as a husband and homecomer — they offer alternative lives (as an animal, as an immortal consort) that would erase who he is. Scylla and Charybdis challenge his identity as a leader who protects his men — he must choose to sacrifice six to save the rest, a decision no good leader should have to make. Even the physical threats carry identity implications: surviving requires the qualities that define Odysseus — cleverness, endurance, restraint. However, the physical threats are genuine — men die horribly, ships are destroyed, and the danger is not merely symbolic. Odysseus's scars and suffering are real.
